subject: Mathematics
title: Arun and Priya's Market Day Mystery
hook: Arun needs to count 40 mangoes fast. Priya shows him a shortcut.

slides.title: The Mango Basket Problem
slides.storyContext: Arun's father owns a fruit shop. Today he received 4 baskets of mangoes, with 8 mangoes in each basket. Arun tries counting on his fingers but gets confused. Priya arrives to help.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Sunday morning at Delhi fruit market. Baskets stacked near the shop counter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arun counts 4 baskets with 8 mangoes each.

image.alt: The Mango Basket Problem — Multiplication

slides.title: Groups and Repeated Addition
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'Instead of counting 8 + 8 + 8 + 8, we can say 4 groups of 8. That's 4 times 8.'

points.label: Idea
points.text: Multiplication means: equal groups of things

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 4 × 8 means 4 groups of 8

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication is quick repeated addition of groups.

image.alt: Groups and Repeated Addition — Multiplication

slides.title: Arun's Mango Count
slides.storyContext: Priya draws 4 circles, puts 8 dots in each. 'See? Add them all: 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32. Or say 4 × 8 = 32.'

example.problem: 4 baskets, 8 mangoes each. How many total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Four times eight equals thirty-two mangoes total.

image.alt: Arun's Mango Count — Multiplication

slides.title: Times Tables Start Here
slides.storyContext: Arun learns: 4 × 1 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 4 × 3 = 12... Priya says, 'It's like counting by 4s: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20...'

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Multiplying by 4: skip count 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32...

slides.inSimpleWords: Times tables are skip counting in equal groups.

image.alt: Times Tables Start Here — Multiplication

slides.title: Priya's Flower Pots
slides.storyContext: Priya mentions her garden: 'I have 6 pots with 3 flowers each. How many flowers do I have?'

example.problem: 6 pots with 3 flowers per pot. Total flowers?
example.solution: 6 × 3 = 18 flowers

slides.inSimpleWords: Six times three is eighteen flowers in total.

image.alt: Priya's Flower Pots — Multiplication

slides.title: Market Challenge
slides.storyContext: Arun's father asks: 'Arun, if I sell 5 bundles of 7 apples each, how many apples do I sell?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Use groups: five groups of seven equals thirty-five.

image.alt: Market Challenge — Multiplication

slides.title: Order Doesn't Matter
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: '4 × 8 is the same as 8 × 4. Both give 32. You can flip the groups around.'

example.problem: Does 3 × 5 equal 5 × 3?
example.solution: Yes! Both = 15. Order of multiplication doesn't change the answer.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip the numbers; multiplication answer stays same.

image.alt: Order Doesn't Matter — Multiplication

slides.title: Arun Masters Multiplication
slides.storyContext: By evening, Arun counts every basket using multiplication. 'Thank you, Priya!' he says. 'Math is like a shortcut at the market!'

points.label: Remember
points.text: Multiplication = equal groups added fast

points.label: Remember
points.text: 4 × 8 means 4 groups of 8

points.label: Remember
points.text: 4 × 8 = 8 × 4 (order doesn't matter)

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication makes counting groups quick and easy.

image.alt: Arun Masters Multiplication — Multiplication

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Birthday Cake Puzzle
hook: Priya has 24 candies to share fairly. Arun helps her divide them equally.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: birthday girl with a math puzzle

slides.title: Birthday Party Fair Share
slides.storyContext: Priya's birthday party has 24 chocolates. She wants to give each friend the same number. There are 6 friends (including her). How many chocolates does each friend get? Arun says, 'That's division!'

points.label: Scene
points.text: Priya's home in Mumbai. Colorful table with 24 chocolates piled up.

slides.inSimpleWords: Priya divides chocolates equally among six friends.

image.alt: Birthday Party Fair Share — Division

slides.title: Division Means Sharing
slides.storyContext: Arun explains: 'Division is the opposite of multiplication. Instead of 6 groups of 4, we ask: 24 things in 6 equal groups—how many in each?'

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 24 ÷ 6 means 24 split into 6 equal groups

slides.inSimpleWords: Division shares things equally into groups.

image.alt: Division Means Sharing — Division

slides.title: Sharing the Chocolates
slides.storyContext: Priya makes 6 piles of chocolates, one for each friend. She places them one by one in a circle: first friend, second friend, third... round and round until all 24 are placed.

example.problem: 24 chocolates shared equally among 6 friends. How many per friend?
example.solution: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 chocolates per friend

slides.inSimpleWords: Twenty-four divided by six equals four chocolates.

image.alt: Sharing the Chocolates — Division

slides.title: Division and Multiplication are Opposites
slides.storyContext: Arun says: 'If 6 × 4 = 24, then 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Multiplication groups; division ungroups.'

points.label: Connection
points.text: 6 groups of 4 → multiply: 6 × 4 = 24

points.label: Connection
points.text: 24 things in 6 groups → divide: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 each

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication and division are opposite operations.

image.alt: Division and Multiplication are Opposites — Division

slides.title: Fruit Baskets
slides.storyContext: Priya asks Arun: 'My father packed 20 oranges into 5 baskets equally. How many oranges in each?'

example.problem: 20 oranges divided into 5 equal baskets
example.solution: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 oranges per basket

slides.inSimpleWords: Twenty oranges in five baskets equals four each.

image.alt: Fruit Baskets — Division

slides.title: Division in the Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Arun's mother made 15 rotlis for dinner. The family has 3 people. How many rotlis per person if shared equally?
slides.inSimpleWords: Fifteen divided by three equals five rotlis each.

image.alt: Division in the Kitchen — Division

slides.title: Grouping Instead of Sharing
slides.storyContext: Arun shows another way: 'We have 12 pencils. If we make groups of 3, how many groups?' He counts: 3, 6, 9, 12—that's 4 groups of 3.

example.problem: 12 pencils grouped in bundles of 3. How many bundles?
example.solution: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 bundles

slides.inSimpleWords: Twelve pencils in groups of three make four.

image.alt: Grouping Instead of Sharing — Division

slides.title: Party Success with Division
slides.storyContext: Each friend gets exactly 4 chocolates. Priya smiles. 'Arun, division makes sure everyone gets the same. Fair and square!'

points.label: Remember
points.text: Division shares things equally or makes equal groups

points.label: Remember
points.text: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 means 24 things in 6 equal parts

points.label: Remember
points.text: Division is the opposite of multiplication

slides.inSimpleWords: Division ensures fair, equal sharing among everyone.

image.alt: Party Success with Division — Division

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun and Priya's Pizza Party
hook: One pizza. Two friends. How do they split it fairly?

slides.title: Cutting the Pizza
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya order one pizza. Arun cuts it straight down the middle. 'Now each of us gets one half,' says Priya. 'That's a fraction!'

points.label: Scene
points.text: Pizza place in Bangalore. One round pizza, knife, two hungry kids.

slides.inSimpleWords: One pizza cut into two equal halves for sharing.

image.alt: Cutting the Pizza — Fractions

slides.title: What is a Fraction?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'A fraction is a part of a whole. When we cut the pizza into 2 equal pieces, each piece is 1/2 of the pizza. Numerator (top) is how many pieces. Denominator (bottom) is total pieces.'

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 1/2 means 1 out of 2 equal pieces

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Top number = how many pieces you have

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Bottom number = total pieces in the whole

slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction shows parts of one whole thing.

image.alt: What is a Fraction? — Fractions

slides.title: Halves (1/2)
slides.storyContext: Arun takes one half. Priya takes the other half. Together, 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 whole pizza.

example.problem: One pizza cut into 2 equal halves. Arun eats 1 half. How much of the whole?
example.solution: Arun eats 1/2 of the pizza

slides.inSimpleWords: Each half is one out of two equal pieces.

image.alt: Halves (1/2) — Fractions

slides.title: Thirds (1/3)
slides.storyContext: Next day, Arun, Priya, and Arun's brother come. One pizza. Three friends. 'Cut it into thirds,' says Arun. Each friend gets 1/3 of the pizza.

points.label: Thirds
points.text: 1/3 means 1 out of 3 equal pieces

points.label: Picture
points.text: Pizza divided into 3 equal slices

slides.inSimpleWords: Thirds divide something equally into three pieces.

image.alt: Thirds (1/3) — Fractions

slides.title: Three Friends, Three Thirds Pizza
slides.storyContext: Priya eats 1/3 of the pizza. Arun eats 1/3. Arun's brother eats 1/3. Together: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = the whole pizza.

example.problem: One pizza divided into 3 equal pieces. Each friend gets how much?
example.solution: Each friend gets 1/3 of the pizza

slides.inSimpleWords: Three equal thirds make one complete whole pizza.

image.alt: Three Friends, Three Thirds Pizza — Fractions

slides.title: Quarters (1/4)
slides.storyContext: A week later, Arun, Priya, and two more friends meet. 'Four friends, one pizza,' says Arun. They cut it into 4 equal squares. Each gets 1/4.

points.label: Quarters
points.text: 1/4 means 1 out of 4 equal pieces

slides.inSimpleWords: Quarters split something into four equal parts.

image.alt: Quarters (1/4) — Fractions

slides.title: Chocolate Bar Sharing
slides.storyContext: Arun has a chocolate bar with 8 squares. He gives Priya 2 squares. What fraction did he give her?

points.label: Try this
points.text: 2 out of 8 squares = 2/8. Can you simplify it?

slides.inSimpleWords: Two out of eight equals one fourth of chocolate.

image.alt: Chocolate Bar Sharing — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions Are Everywhere
slides.storyContext: By the end of the week, Arun and Priya see fractions all around: half a glass of milk, a quarter hour on the clock, three-quarters of a tank full.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Fraction = one or more equal parts of a whole

points.label: Remember
points.text: 1/2 (half), 1/3 (third), 1/4 (quarter) are common

points.label: Remember
points.text: Bottom number = how many equal pieces total

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole in daily life.

image.alt: Fractions Are Everywhere — Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's Lemonade Stand and Priya's Shop
hook: Arun sells lemonade. Priya buys. Can they count money correctly?

slides.title: Summer Lemonade Business
slides.storyContext: It is summer in Delhi. Arun sets up a lemonade stand with Priya's help. A glass costs 5 rupees. On day one, Arun sells 8 glasses. How much money does he earn? Priya pulls out her notebook to calculate.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Street corner. Hot day. Colorful lemonade stand. Line of customers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arun and Priya run a lemonade stand together.

image.alt: Summer Lemonade Business — Money

slides.title: Indian Money: Rupees and Paise
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'In India, we use rupees (Rs). 100 paise = 1 rupee. Coins: 1 Rs, 2 Rs, 5 Rs, 10 Rs. Notes: 10 Rs, 20 Rs, 50 Rs, 100 Rs.' Arun nods, counting his coins.

points.label: Value
points.text: 100 paise = 1 rupee

points.label: Coins
points.text: 1 Rs, 2 Rs, 5 Rs, 10 Rs are common

points.label: Notes
points.text: 10 Rs, 20 Rs, 50 Rs, 100 Rs are used daily

slides.inSimpleWords: One rupee equals one hundred paise always.

image.alt: Indian Money: Rupees and Paise — Money

slides.title: Arun's Daily Earnings
slides.storyContext: Arun sold 8 glasses at 5 Rs each. 'That is 8 times 5,' says Priya. They count: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 40 Rs. Arun earns 40 rupees in one day.

example.problem: 8 glasses at 5 Rs each. Total earnings?
example.solution: 8 × 5 = 40 rupees

slides.inSimpleWords: Eight glasses times five rupees equals forty total.

image.alt: Arun's Daily Earnings — Money

slides.title: Adding Money
slides.storyContext: Arun earns 40 Rs on day one, 50 Rs on day two, and 35 Rs on day three. 'How much altogether?' asks Priya. She adds: 40 + 50 + 35 = 125 Rs.

points.label: Add
points.text: 40 Rs + 50 Rs + 35 Rs = 125 Rs

points.label: Method
points.text: Line up the rupees and add

slides.inSimpleWords: Add rupees together like regular numbers.

image.alt: Adding Money — Money

slides.title: Buying Supplies
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya visit the market. Lemons cost 20 Rs per kilogram. Sugar: 15 Rs. Bottles: 30 Rs. Total cost for supplies: 20 + 15 + 30 = 65 Rs. 'We spend 65 Rs,' says Priya.

example.problem: Lemons (20 Rs) + sugar (15 Rs) + bottles (30 Rs) = ?
example.solution: 20 + 15 + 30 = 65 rupees total cost

slides.inSimpleWords: Twenty plus fifteen plus thirty equals sixty-five.

image.alt: Buying Supplies — Money

slides.title: Profit and Money Left
slides.storyContext: Arun earned 40 Rs on day one. He spent 65 Rs on supplies. 'Do we have enough?' asks Priya. 'After day two we will!' says Arun. 40 + 50 = 90 Rs, minus 65 Rs cost = 25 Rs profit.

points.label: Profit
points.text: Money earned minus money spent = profit

slides.inSimpleWords: Profit equals earnings minus the cost of supplies.

image.alt: Profit and Money Left — Money

slides.title: Arun Wants a Prize
slides.storyContext: Arun sees a toy for 100 Rs. He earned 125 Rs total. If he spends 100 Rs on the toy, how much money does he have left?
slides.inSimpleWords: One hundred twenty-five minus one hundred equals twenty-five.

image.alt: Arun Wants a Prize — Money

slides.title: Arun and Priya's Success
slides.storyContext: By end of summer, Arun bought the toy and still has 25 Rs left. 'We learned addition, subtraction, and money together,' says Priya. 'And multiplication too!' adds Arun.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Money has units: rupees and paise

points.label: Remember
points.text: Add and subtract money like regular numbers

points.label: Remember
points.text: Profit = earnings minus costs

slides.inSimpleWords: Using math with money helps you earn and save.

image.alt: Arun and Priya's Success — Money

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun's School Day with Priya's Clock
hook: What time does school start? How long until lunch? Arun learns to read the clock.

slides.title: Learning to Read the Clock
slides.storyContext: Arun's school day starts at 9:00 AM. He keeps asking Priya, 'Is it time for lunch yet?' By the fifth time, Priya says, 'Arun, I will teach you to read the clock so you can check yourself!'

points.label: Scene
points.text: Classroom. Big wall clock. Priya pointing at the numbers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arun wants to know when lunch time arrives each day.

image.alt: Learning to Read the Clock — Time and Calendar

slides.title: The Analog Clock Face
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'A clock has 12 numbers. The short hand shows the hour (like 9 for 9 o'clock). The long hand shows the minutes. It takes 60 minutes to make one full circle.'

points.label: Short hand
points.text: Hour hand—shows which hour (1 to 12)

points.label: Long hand
points.text: Minute hand—shows which minute (0 to 60)

points.label: 60 minutes
points.text: = 1 hour exactly

slides.inSimpleWords: A clock has two hands showing hours and minutes.

image.alt: The Analog Clock Face — Time and Calendar

slides.title: 9 o'Clock: School Starts
slides.storyContext: Priya points: 'When the short hand points to 9 and the long hand points to 12, it is 9:00 o'clock. School starts.'

example.problem: What time does the clock show: short hand at 9, long hand at 12?
example.solution: 9:00 o'clock (9 AM)

slides.inSimpleWords: When both hands point up, it is exactly nine.

image.alt: 9 o'Clock: School Starts — Time and Calendar

slides.title: Minutes Past the Hour
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: 'When the long hand moves to 3, it means 15 minutes past. To 6 means 30 minutes past. To 9 means 45 minutes past.'

points.label: At 3
points.text: 15 minutes past the hour

points.label: At 6
points.text: 30 minutes past (half past)

points.label: At 9
points.text: 45 minutes past (quarter to next hour)

slides.inSimpleWords: Different positions of the minute hand show minutes.

image.alt: Minutes Past the Hour — Time and Calendar

slides.title: 10:30 AM: Snack Time
slides.storyContext: The bell rings. Priya checks the clock: short hand between 10 and 11, long hand at 6. 'It is 10:30! Half past 10. Snack time, Arun!'

example.problem: Short hand between 10 and 11, long hand at 6. What time?
example.solution: 10:30 (half past 10)

slides.inSimpleWords: The hand at six means thirty minutes past the hour.

image.alt: 10:30 AM: Snack Time — Time and Calendar

slides.title: Days and Months
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a calendar. 'Look, there are 7 days in a week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday... And 12 months in a year: January, February...' Arun points to June: 'That is summer!'

points.label: Days
points.text: 7 days per week (Monday to Sunday)

points.label: Months
points.text: 12 months per year (January to December)

points.label: Dates
points.text: Days have numbers: 1 to 31

slides.inSimpleWords: Calendars show all days, weeks, and months.

image.alt: Days and Months — Time and Calendar

slides.title: What Time is Lunch?
slides.storyContext: Arun checks the clock himself. Short hand at 1, long hand at 12. 'Is it lunch time (1:00 PM)?' he asks Priya. She nods with a smile.

points.label: Try this
points.text: If school ends at 3:30 PM, where should the hands point?

slides.inSimpleWords: The short hand at one means one o'clock exactly.

image.alt: What Time is Lunch? — Time and Calendar

slides.title: Arun Never Asks Again
slides.storyContext: From that day on, Arun reads the clock himself. 'Priya, remember when you taught me? Now I am the time keeper!' He checks his watch proud, ready for every activity.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Short hand = hour (1 to 12), long hand = minute (0 to 60)

points.label: Remember
points.text: 60 minutes = 1 hour, 7 days = 1 week, 12 months = 1 year

points.label: Remember
points.text: Read the short hand first, then the long hand

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading clocks helps you be on time always.

image.alt: Arun Never Asks Again — Time and Calendar

subject: Science
title: Arun's Garden and Priya's Plant Discovery
hook: Why do plants need roots? Priya digs deep to find out.

slides.title: Digging Up a Plant
slides.storyContext: Arun digs up a tomato plant from his garden. Priya sees roots, a thick stem, green leaves, and yellow flowers. 'Why does a plant have so many different parts?' she asks.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Arun's backyard garden in Pune. Soil, shovel, a tomato plant freshly pulled up.

slides.inSimpleWords: A plant has many parts, each with its own job.

image.alt: Digging Up a Plant — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Roots: Drink Water and Hold On
slides.storyContext: Priya observes the roots—thin, thread-like strands underground. 'Roots drink water from the soil and hold the plant in the ground,' explains Arun. 'If I pull at the stem, the roots hold tight!'

points.label: Job 1
points.text: Absorb water and nutrients from soil

points.label: Job 2
points.text: Keep the plant anchored in the ground

points.label: Where
points.text: Roots grow underground

slides.inSimpleWords: Roots drink water and anchor plants firmly down.

image.alt: Roots: Drink Water and Hold On — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Two Types of Roots
slides.storyContext: Priya asks, 'Why do some plants have thick roots like carrots, and others have thin thread-like roots?' Arun explains: 'This tomato has fibrous roots (many thin ones). A carrot has a taproot (one thick one that goes deep).'

example.problem: Why might a carrot store food in its root?
example.solution: The taproot stores nutrients to survive. That is why carrots are orange and crunchy!

slides.inSimpleWords: Different plants have different kinds of roots.

image.alt: Two Types of Roots — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Stem: Transport and Support
slides.storyContext: Priya feels the thick green stem of the tomato plant. 'The stem carries water from the roots to the leaves. It also holds up the leaves so they can catch sunlight,' says Arun.

points.label: Job 1
points.text: Transport water and nutrients to leaves and flowers

points.label: Job 2
points.text: Support the plant's weight

points.label: Example
points.text: A tree's trunk is its stem

slides.inSimpleWords: The stem carries water up and holds leaves high.

image.alt: Stem: Transport and Support — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Leaves: Make Food for the Plant
slides.storyContext: Priya touches a green leaf. 'Why are leaves green?' she asks. Arun replies, 'Green is chlorophyll. It helps leaves catch sunlight and make food for the plant. Without leaves, the plant would starve!'

example.problem: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard for a month. What happens?
example.solution: Without sunlight, leaves cannot make food. The plant dies or turns yellow/white.

slides.inSimpleWords: Green leaves make food using sunlight every day.

image.alt: Leaves: Make Food for the Plant — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Flowers and Fruits: Make Seeds
slides.storyContext: Priya points to yellow flowers on the tomato plant. 'When flowers are pollinated by bees, they make fruits. Inside fruits are seeds,' explains Arun. 'Seeds grow into new plants!'

points.label: Flowers
points.text: Attract bees and butterflies for pollination

points.label: Fruits
points.text: Protect seeds inside

points.label: Seeds
points.text: Grow into new plants (reproduction)

slides.inSimpleWords: Flowers become fruits, and fruits hold seeds inside.

image.alt: Flowers and Fruits: Make Seeds — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Plant Needs Detective
slides.storyContext: Priya takes a plant and: (1) Hides its roots in dark soil, (2) Puts it near a window, (3) Waters it daily. 'What does it need to grow?' she asks. Arun says, 'All three!'

points.label: Try this
points.text: What happens if a plant gets no water? No sunlight? No soil?

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants need soil, water, sunlight, and air daily.

image.alt: Plant Needs Detective — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Arun and Priya's Plant Wisdom
slides.storyContext: By season's end, both have learned: roots, stem, leaves, flowers, and fruits all work together. Each part has its job. A healthy plant is a team of parts!

points.label: Remember
points.text: Roots: absorb water, anchor plant

points.label: Remember
points.text: Stem: transport water, support leaves

points.label: Remember
points.text: Leaves: make food using sunlight

points.label: Remember
points.text: Flowers and fruits: make seeds for new plants

slides.inSimpleWords: Each plant part does a special job for survival.

image.alt: Arun and Priya's Plant Wisdom — Plants - Parts and Functions

subject: Science
title: Arun's Backyard Explorer Journey with Priya
hook: Arun finds a bird, a butterfly, and a fish. What do they have in common? What makes them different?

slides.title: A Curious Morning at the Pond
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya visit a garden pond. A sparrow lands on a branch. A butterfly flutters by. Fish ripple the water below. 'They are all animals, but so different!' says Arun. 'Let us explore,' says Priya.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Garden in Mumbai. Pond with lily pads. Trees with birds. Flowers with insects.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different animals live in different parts of nature.

image.alt: A Curious Morning at the Pond — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

slides.title: Birds: Built to Fly
slides.storyContext: Priya describes the sparrow: 'Birds have feathers (light and strong), two wings (for flying), two legs (for standing), and lay eggs. They breathe air with lungs.'

points.label: Feathers
points.text: Lightweight, waterproof, keep birds warm

points.label: Wings
points.text: Two wings for flying (or swimming like penguins)

points.label: Eggs
points.text: Birds lay eggs with hard shells

points.label: Breathing
points.text: Lungs; they live on land and in air

slides.inSimpleWords: Birds have feathers, wings, and lay eggs in nests.

image.alt: Birds: Built to Fly — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

slides.title: Sparrow vs Penguin
slides.storyContext: Arun asks, 'Do all birds fly?' Priya explains: 'A sparrow flies. A penguin has wings but cannot fly—it swims instead. Both are birds because they have feathers and lay eggs.'

example.problem: A penguin has feathers and wings but cannot fly. Is it still a bird?
example.solution: Yes! A bird is defined by feathers, wings, and laying eggs—not always by flying.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some birds fly, but all birds have feathers.

image.alt: Sparrow vs Penguin — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

slides.title: Insects: Six Legs and Exoskeletons
slides.storyContext: Priya catches a butterfly gently. 'Look! Six legs. Three body parts: head, thorax (middle), abdomen (rear). And wings!' Arun counts: 'One, two, three, four, five, six. Yes, six!'

points.label: Legs
points.text: Insects have exactly 6 legs (that is how you know!)

points.label: Body
points.text: Three parts: head, thorax, abdomen

points.label: Wings
points.text: Some insects have 2 or 4 wings

points.label: Growth
points.text: Many insects change shape (metamorphosis)

slides.inSimpleWords: Insects have six legs and three body sections always.

image.alt: Insects: Six Legs and Exoskeletons — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

slides.title: Butterfly Transformation
slides.storyContext: Priya tells Arun: 'A butterfly starts as an egg, becomes a caterpillar (lots of legs but not 6), then a chrysalis, then a butterfly (6 legs). It is metamorphosis!'

example.problem: A caterpillar has 8 pairs of legs. A butterfly has 3 pairs. Why the difference?
example.solution: Caterpillars and butterflies are different life stages of the same animal. Metamorphosis changes them completely.

slides.inSimpleWords: Butterflies transform from caterpillars in stages.

image.alt: Butterfly Transformation — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

slides.title: Fish: Scales, Fins, Gills
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya peer into the pond. A goldfish glides by. 'Scales protect the fish. Fins help it swim. Gills help it breathe underwater,' explains Priya.

points.label: Scales
points.text: Protect the fish, keep it waterproof

points.label: Fins
points.text: Help fish swim (dorsal, tail, pectoral fins)

points.label: Gills
points.text: Extract oxygen from water to breathe

points.label: Eggs
points.text: Fish lay eggs in water

slides.inSimpleWords: Fish have scales, fins, and gills for water life.

image.alt: Fish: Scales, Fins, Gills — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

slides.title: Classify the Creatures
slides.storyContext: Arun finds: a dragonfly, a crow, a ladybug, and a frog in the pond. 'Classify each as bird, insect, or fish,' says Priya. Arun counts legs on each: dragonfly (6 = insect), crow (2 = bird), ladybug (6 = insect), frog (0 fish, 4 legs = neither!).

points.label: Try this
points.text: How many legs has each creature? Does it match bird, insect, or fish traits?

slides.inSimpleWords: Count legs and check for feathers, scales, or wings.

image.alt: Classify the Creatures — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

slides.title: Nature's Diversity
slides.storyContext: By day's end, Arun and Priya understand: birds fly with feathers, insects crawl on 6 legs, fish swim with fins and gills. Each is perfectly built for its home.

points.label: Birds
points.text: Feathers, wings, 2 legs, lay eggs, breathe air

points.label: Insects
points.text: 6 legs, 3 body parts, some have wings, lay eggs

points.label: Fish
points.text: Scales, fins, gills, breathe water, lay eggs

slides.inSimpleWords: Different animals are built for different environments.

image.alt: Nature's Diversity — Animals - Birds, Insects, Fish

subject: Science
title: Arun and Priya's Body Discoveries
hook: How do we see, hear, and feel? Arun and Priya explore their own bodies.

slides.title: What Makes Us Move?
slides.storyContext: Arun plays cricket, hitting a ball hard. His arm moves, his legs run, his eyes follow the ball. 'Priya, why can I do all this?' Priya smiles. 'Your bones, muscles, nerves, and senses all work together!'

points.label: Scene
points.text: Cricket field in Bangalore. Arun batting. Priya sitting on the sidelines with notebook.

slides.inSimpleWords: Our body is a team of bones, muscles, and nerves.

image.alt: What Makes Us Move? — Our Body

slides.title: Bones: The Frame
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'Your skeleton has 206 bones (in adults). Bones support your body, protect your organs (like your brain inside your skull), and help you move. Feel your ribs—they protect your heart and lungs!'

points.label: Support
points.text: Bones hold your body upright

points.label: Protection
points.text: Skull protects brain, ribs protect heart/lungs

points.label: Movement
points.text: Bones work with muscles to move your body

points.label: Storage
points.text: Bones store calcium and other minerals

slides.inSimpleWords: Bones form a frame that supports and protects.

image.alt: Bones: The Frame — Our Body

slides.title: Muscles: The Movers
slides.storyContext: Arun flexes his arm. Priya touches his bicep muscle: 'When this muscle contracts (gets shorter), your arm bends. When it relaxes, your arm straightens. Muscles always work in pairs!'

example.problem: Why do muscles work in pairs?
example.solution: One muscle bends (contracts), the other straightens (relaxes). Without both, movement would not work. Biceps bend the arm; triceps straighten it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Muscles pull bones to make your body move.

image.alt: Muscles: The Movers — Our Body

slides.title: The Five Senses
slides.storyContext: Priya describes each sense: Eyes (sight), Ears (hearing), Nose (smell), Tongue (taste), Skin (touch). 'Your senses send messages to your brain through nerves. Your brain makes sense of the world!'

points.label: Eyes
points.text: See light and colors

points.label: Ears
points.text: Hear sounds and vibrations

points.label: Nose
points.text: Smell odors in the air

points.label: Tongue
points.text: Taste sweet, salty, sour, bitter

points.label: Skin
points.text: Feel hot, cold, rough, smooth, pain

slides.inSimpleWords: Five senses let us experience the whole world.

image.alt: The Five Senses — Our Body

slides.title: The Reflex Arc
slides.storyContext: Arun touches a hot plate accidentally. His hand pulls back instantly—before his brain even knows! 'That is a reflex,' explains Priya. 'A nerve signal goes down to your spinal cord, which tells muscles to move fast, protecting you.'

example.problem: Why does your hand pull away from a hot thing before you feel pain?
example.solution: Reflexes are automatic. Nerves in your hand connect to the spinal cord, triggering muscles instantly—faster than thinking.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reflexes protect us from danger without thinking.

image.alt: The Reflex Arc — Our Body

slides.title: Heart and Lungs: Life Engines
slides.storyContext: Priya places her hand on Arun's chest after he runs. 'Feel your heartbeat? Your heart pumps blood to every part of your body. Your lungs breathe air. Together, they give your body oxygen and energy!'

points.label: Heart
points.text: Pumps blood carrying oxygen to the whole body

points.label: Lungs
points.text: Take in oxygen from air, remove carbon dioxide

points.label: Blood
points.text: Carries oxygen and nutrients everywhere

slides.inSimpleWords: Your heart and lungs keep you alive every moment.

image.alt: Heart and Lungs: Life Engines — Our Body

slides.title: Body Race
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya run around the garden. Arun counts his heartbeats: 60 at rest, 120 after running. 'Why does your heart beat faster when you exercise?' asks Priya. Arun answers: 'Muscles need more oxygen and blood!'

points.label: Try this
points.text: Count your resting heartbeats. Then run. Count again. How much did it increase?

slides.inSimpleWords: Exercise makes your heart pump faster for oxygen.

image.alt: Body Race — Our Body

slides.title: Arun's Body Blueprint
slides.storyContext: Arun now understands: his skeleton and muscles move him, his senses let him explore, his heart and lungs keep him alive, and his nerves connect it all. His body is amazing!

points.label: Remember
points.text: Bones support and protect; muscles move them

points.label: Remember
points.text: Five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch

points.label: Remember
points.text: Heart pumps blood; lungs breathe air

points.label: Remember
points.text: Nerves connect everything and send messages

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body is an amazing team of systems.

image.alt: Arun's Body Blueprint — Our Body

subject: Science
title: Arun and Priya's Shadow Theater
hook: Can you make shadows dance? Arun and Priya explore light and dark.

slides.title: The Puppet Show
slides.storyContext: On a rainy evening, Arun and Priya set up a shadow puppet show. Priya holds a lamp. Arun makes hand shapes between the lamp and a white sheet. Giant shadows dance on the wall. 'How does this work?' asks Arun.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Arun's house. White sheet hung on wall. Lamp behind Arun. Dark room.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light makes shadows when blocked by objects.

image.alt: The Puppet Show — Light and Shadow

slides.title: What is Light?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'Light travels in straight lines from a source (like the sun or a lamp). When light hits an object, it can pass through (transparent), bend through (transparent-ish), or bounce off (opaque/reflective).'

points.label: Transparent
points.text: Light passes through—you see clearly (glass, water)

points.label: Translucent
points.text: Light bends through—blurry view (frosted glass)

points.label: Opaque
points.text: Light bounces off—you cannot see through (wood, paper)

slides.inSimpleWords: Light travels straight and bounces off things.

image.alt: What is Light? — Light and Shadow

slides.title: How Shadows Form
slides.storyContext: Arun holds his hand up to the lamp. 'Light goes straight from the lamp, hits my hand (opaque), and cannot go through. Behind my hand, there is no light—a shadow!'

example.problem: Why is there a shadow behind an opaque object in a light beam?
example.solution: Light travels in straight lines. When it hits an opaque object, it cannot pass through, creating a dark area (shadow) behind it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadows form when objects block light rays.

image.alt: How Shadows Form — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Shadow Sizes Change
slides.storyContext: Priya moves the lamp closer to Arun's hand. His shadow gets bigger. 'The closer the light source, the bigger the shadow because light spreads out from a point!'

points.label: Close light
points.text: Bigger shadow

points.label: Far light
points.text: Smaller shadow

points.label: Reason
points.text: Light rays spread wider from close source

slides.inSimpleWords: Light distance changes the size of shadows.

image.alt: Shadow Sizes Change — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Sun Shadows During the Day
slides.storyContext: Priya says, 'The sun creates your shadow outdoors. In the morning, your shadow is long. At noon, it is short. In the evening, it is long again. Why?' Arun figures out: 'Because the sun is angle changes!'

example.problem: Why is your shadow longest in early morning and late evening?
example.solution: When the sun is low on the horizon, light rays hit at an angle, making shadows stretch. At noon, the sun is high, shadows are short.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sun angle changes shadow size throughout the day.

image.alt: Sun Shadows During the Day — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Reflection: Light Bounces
slides.storyContext: Priya holds a mirror in Arun's light beam. 'Look! The light bounces off the mirror and reflects. Mirrors are very smooth and shiny, so light bounces perfectly.'

points.label: Reflection
points.text: Light bounces off smooth, shiny surfaces (mirrors)

points.label: Angle
points.text: Light bounces at the same angle it hits (angle of incidence = angle of reflection)

points.label: Diffuse
points.text: Rough surfaces scatter light in all directions

slides.inSimpleWords: Mirrors reflect light back instead of absorbing it.

image.alt: Reflection: Light Bounces — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Create Shadow Art
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya stage a shadow puppet show: a dog, a butterfly, a bird. 'Make bigger shadows, smaller shadows, moving shadows!' says Priya. Arun practices different hand shapes and lamp distances.

points.label: Try this
points.text: Make 5 different animal shadows using your hands and a light source.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadow puppets show how light and objects interact.

image.alt: Create Shadow Art — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Light and Shadow Mastery
slides.storyContext: By night's end, Arun and Priya have created a complete puppet story. They now know: light travels straight, shadows form when light is blocked, and mirrors reflect light. Magic is just science!

points.label: Remember
points.text: Light travels in straight lines from a source

points.label: Remember
points.text: Shadows form behind opaque objects blocking light

points.label: Remember
points.text: Shadow size depends on light distance and angle

points.label: Remember
points.text: Mirrors reflect light; rough surfaces scatter it

slides.inSimpleWords: Light, shadows, and reflection create amazing effects.

image.alt: Light and Shadow Mastery — Light and Shadow
